scene_jp: <ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby><ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>のコンコースは、<ruby>何千<rt>なんぜん</rt></ruby>もの<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>でにぎわっていた。アナウンスの<ruby>声<rt>こえ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>天井<rt>てんじょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>響<rt>ひび</rt></ruby>き、<ruby>足音<rt>あしおと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>波<rt>なみ</rt></ruby>のように<ruby>重<rt>かさ</rt></ruby>なり<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う。そのとき、<ruby>売店<rt>ばいてん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>っている<ruby>老<rt>ろう</rt></ruby>じんが、こちらをじっと<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ていることに<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>がついた。<ruby>老<rt>ろう</rt></ruby>じんはゆっくりと<ruby>近<rt>ちか</rt></ruby>づいてきて、「テストさん、<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>の<ruby>出口<rt>でぐち</rt></ruby>で<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>か<ruby>拾<rt>ひろ</rt></ruby>いましたね」と、まるで<ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby><ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>っていたかのように<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かに<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>った。<ruby>老<rt>ろう</rt></ruby>じんの<ruby>手<rt>て</rt></ruby>には、<ruby>同<rt>おな</rt></ruby>じ<ruby>紙<rt>かみ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>かれたメモが<ruby>握<rt>にぎ</rt></ruby>られていた——<ruby>半分<rt>はんぶん</rt></ruby>だけ。
scene_translation: Tokyo Station's concourse buzzed with thousands of people. Announcement voices echoed off the high ceiling, and the sound of footsteps layered together like waves. Just then, you noticed an old man standing in front of a kiosk, staring steadily in your direction. He slowly approached and said quietly, as though he already knew everything: 'You picked something up at the station exit, didn't you, テスト.' In his hand was a memo written on the same kind of paper — but only half of it.
grammar_note: 【まるで〜かのように】means 'as if' or 'just like' — it compares something to an imagined situation. まるで is often paired with かのように (or ように alone) to add a dreamlike, unreal quality. Example from the scene: まるで全部知っていたかのように静かに言った — 'he said quietly, as if he had known everything all along.' The かのように form (using か + の + よう) is slightly more formal and literary than ように alone.

vocab.meaning: to layer on top of each other, to overlap
to grip, to hold in one's hand

mystery_memo: The old man at the kiosk knows the player's name and knows they picked something up at the station exit — he should not know either of these things. He holds the other half of a memo written on the same paper as whatever was found at the exit, suggesting the note was deliberately split. This is the second time the player's name has been used by a stranger. The old man's relationship is currently neutral-unknown; his tone is polite but unsettling. The two memo halves together may form a key clue.
